# Decision fixtures

Reference numbers for the decision models served on `/v1/systemone`, recorded
from the decision server of the vendored llama.cpp fork by
`scripts/decision-golden.sh`. They are what a decision implementation in this
repository has to reproduce.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `requests.json` | the frozen request set of the marker readouts, `/v1/systemone` bodies |
| `requests-<family>.json` | the frozen request set of another readout family (below) |
| `golden-<model>.<backend>.json` | the reference for one model on one backend; a CPU backend is named after its architecture (`cpu-x86_64`, `cpu-aarch64`) |
| `TINYLAYA_FIXTURE.toml` | the manifest of the small test model, fetched by `scripts/fetch-cpu-fixture.sh decision/TINYLAYA_FIXTURE` |

## The requests

| Name | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `reference_example` | the request of the upstream pull request: an object state, a 4-option choice, a noul with and without criteria, a 4-level score, a 10-option choice with `null` descriptions |
| `text_state_null_descriptions` | a text state, a choice mixing a description and `null` ones |
| `marker_text_in_inputs` | the marker text (`<mask>`) in the state, the instructions, a description and an option key: it is replaced before rendering |
| `twenty_long_options` | 20 long options: every option is cut, then all are shrunk evenly to the head budget |
| `score_ten_levels` | a 10-level score, an array state |
| `long_question_model_budget` | a question and options over the head budget, with the budget of the model |
| `long_question_budget_512` | the same request with the budget at 512, the override the configuration may set |

`llama-server` reads the budget from the model only, so the last entry is
recorded by the capture tool and not replayed against the server.

The other readout families are recorded on tiny models generated by
`scripts/gen-tiny-decision-fixture.py --type NAME` (random F32 weights, a
`systemone` template written for the fixture, the metadata the type reads;
their answers mean nothing), each with the request file of its family:

| Request file | Models (`golden-tiny-<type>`) | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `requests-labels.json` | `openjev` (letters), `lev` (codes, two orders, rating scale), `nimble` (all the questions listed), `vllm-d3` (null state and instructions, canonical legend, entropy confidence), `lfm2-d1` and `lfm3-d1` (label groups, letter keys, special token texts broken, median score) | object, text and array states; descriptions that are null, text, objects and numbers; 30 options (refused by the code readouts, coded from the pool by the d1 ones); a refused null state |
| `requests-h2o.json` | `h2o-lightning` | the Python rendering (`json.dumps` of the instructions and descriptions, `repr` of floats, the strip of the last option), the quoting of special token texts, the default type and instructions, `yes`/`no` descriptions, more options than labels |
| `requests-joint.json` | `clef` (every question in one prompt), `vllm-decision2` (one prompt per question, strict payloads) | the decision order of each span, sorted keys, the marker text in the input, the refusals of empty instructions and of a single option |
| `requests-kev.json` | `kev`, and `Kev-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf` opt-in | inputs flattened to text, the numbers as the server writes them (`4.69895e20`, `1.5e-7`, `1e15`, `100000.0`), end-token texts escaped |
| `requests-d1omni.json` | `lfm2-d1-omni` (the laya encoder of the generated laya model, read with the d1-omni layout) | the pieces cut to their budgets, escapes, `no`/`yes` descriptions, a null state |

The generated laya model (`TINY_DECISION_FIXTURE.toml`) is recorded with
`requests.json` as `golden-tiny-laya`.

`openbmb-minicpm-ocr-jev` needs two images per request and has no recording:
without a multimodal projector every request it accepts is answered 501.
`pplx-decider`, `granite-switch` and `lfm3-d1-omni` differ from a recorded
type only by a row of `readout::DECISION_TYPES` (their media, the order of a
`noul`).

A refused request records the message llama-server answers with (`error`).

## What a golden file holds

For each request: the head budget used (a marker readout), and per forward
pass (`questions`: one per variant of a question, or one for every question of
a `clef` prompt, `id` null) the rendered prompt (`prompt`), its tokens
(`rendered_tokens`, or `pieces` for a layout that tokenizes the prompt piece by
piece), the tokens after the layout (`tokens`), where the scores are read
(`markers`, `column`, `pointer`, `labels` and `label_groups`, the decision
`order` of each token and `n_scores` of a joint head), the raw scores, and the
server response (`answers`, `usage`). `model.readout` holds what the readout
read from the model (labels, marker, quoted spellings, temperatures), so the
logic can be replayed without it. The model file is identified by name and
SHA-256; the files themselves are never committed.

| Model | Readout | Head budget in the file | Opt-in variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tinylaya` (Q8_0, 97 MB, Apache-2.0) | `laya` | 192 | always, `RETRO_TINYLAYA_FIXTURE` to relocate it |
| `julia-1` (`Julia-1-Q8_0.gguf`, Apache-2.0) | `laya` | 256 | `RETRO_DECISION_JULIA` |
| `laya` (`Laya-Q8_0.gguf`, Apache-2.0) | `laya` | 192 | `RETRO_DECISION_LAYA` |
| `kev` (`Kev-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf`, Apache-2.0) | `kev` | - | `RETRO_DECISION_KEV` |
| `tiny-laya` (`TINY_DECISION_FIXTURE.toml`, generated) | `laya` | 64 | always, `RETRO_TINY_DECISION_FIXTURE` to relocate it |
| `tiny-<type>` (generated, about 500 KB each) | `<type>` | - | always |

## Tolerance

The CPU references are built as the workspace builds its CPU backend: no BLAS,
no Accelerate, no host-specific instructions (`scripts/decision-golden/CMakeLists.txt`).
llama.cpp's default macOS build multiplies matrices through Accelerate, which
changes the arithmetic; a reference the workspace cannot run the kernels of is
not one it can match. The Metal references do not depend on these options.

Measured on the recorded files (Apple M-series, CPU and Metal backends; and
an x86_64 CPU):

| Comparison | Largest probability difference |
|---|---|
| capture tool against `llama-server` built the same way, same backend | 0 (same code, same kernels) |
| two runs, same backend | 0 |
| CPU against Metal, `tinylaya` Q8_0 | 1.2e-3 |
| CPU against Metal, `laya` Q8_0 | 1.1e-1 (`twenty_long_options`, two near-tied options) |
| CPU against Metal, `julia-1` Q8_0 | 3.1e-1, and one choice changes |
| this CPU build against llama.cpp's default (Accelerate) build | `tinylaya` 3.8e-4, `laya` 4.9e-2, `julia-1` 3.6e-1 (two choices change) |
| CPU against Metal, `julia-1` BF16, default build | 2.7e-2 |
| `julia-1` Q8_0 against BF16, CPU, default build | 2.6e-1 |
| CPU x86_64 against CPU aarch64 (Apple), same options | `tinylaya` 1.3e-3, `laya` 7.3e-2, `julia-1` 1.7e-1 |
| capture tool against `llama-server`, x86_64 CPU, every pass the server evaluates whole (13 models) | 0 |
| a pass `llama-server` evaluates after the prefix it kept from the previous pass of its request (causal tiny models) | up to 9.7e-4 |

What follows from it:

- **Same weights, same backend: 1e-3**, and a parity test compares against the
  golden file of its own backend. Tokens, markers and usage are exact on any
  backend: they do not depend on arithmetic.
- **Across backends there is no single tolerance.** The CPU quantizes the
  activations of a Q8_0 matrix product to Q8_0, Metal keeps them in F32, and
  Julia-1's head amplifies the difference far beyond what Laya's does. The
  upstream pull request reports the same fragility (Julia-1 is its worst model
  against the PyTorch reference, 2.2e-2, measured on a higher-precision file).
- Laya on Metal reproduces the values the upstream pull request reports for
  `reference_example` within 1.4e-3, and its token count (414) exactly.
- The head budget changes answers: on Metal (and on the default CPU build),
  Julia-1 picks `legal` on `long_question_model_budget` (256) and `support` with
  512. The value in the model file is the default for that reason.
